opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. I think what's really interesting is that language has gotten so much of the attention over the last few years, and for good reason; it's been incredibly successful. But when you step back and think about how intelligence actually works, both in people and in animals, so much of it isn't linguistic at all. It's about understanding the three-dimensional world you live in: where things are, how they move, how they'd look from a different angle, what happens if you push on something or walk around a corner.

Language is a pretty lossy, one-dimensional channel for describing that. If I try to tell you in words exactly how to tie a knot, or the layout of a room, it's awkward. But if you can just see it and reason about it spatially, it's immediate. So a lot of the interest for me is the question: what happens if you build models whose native representation is the 3D world itself, rather than tokens of text? What kinds of capabilities fall out of that, for generation, for robotics, for design, for anything where you need to interact with physical space?

There's also a scientific angle. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years building visual and spatial intelligence before anything like language showed up. That suggests spatial understanding is a really deep foundation, and it's not obvious you get it for free just by scaling language models. So to me it's both an exciting technical problem, since 3D has all these hard questions about representation, data, and consistency, and a bet that this is one of the next big frontiers for AI.

r003.rationale: It contrasts 3D-world representations with text tokens, but does not suggest that a model could develop an accurate account of physics using different notation.

r004.rationale: It calls language a lossy channel for describing spatial information, but does not say that human language structure constrains outputs from models using other modalities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's really interesting to me is that when you look at the history of intelligence on this planet, language is incredibly recent. Animals have been navigating 3D space, perceiving the world, manipulating objects, for hundreds of millions of years, and that's all happening without language. Language is this very thin layer on top of a much deeper substrate of spatial understanding.

And the LLM revolution has been incredible, but in some sense language is the easy modality for machine learning, because humans already did the compression for you. Text is this highly structured, already-abstracted representation of the world. Pixels are not like that. The raw sensory input is enormously high-dimensional, it's noisy, and the structure you care about — that there's a 3D world out there, that objects persist, that things have physical extent and occlude each other — none of that is written down anywhere. The model has to discover it.

So the intellectual question for me is: can you build a system that learns a rich model of the world primarily from visual and spatial data, the way a child or an animal does, rather than inheriting that structure secondhand through text? Because I think a lot of what we call common sense is actually spatial. If I ask you whether a cup will fall off the edge of a table, you're not reasoning over sentences, you're running a little simulation in your head. And current language models are weirdly bad at exactly those kinds of questions, because they've only ever seen descriptions of the world, not the world itself.

There's also a practical side. If you want models that act in the physical world — robots, AR, anything embodied — they need to be grounded in geometry. A model that can generate a coherent 3D scene, keep track of where things are as the viewpoint moves, reason about what's behind the thing in front of it — that's the foundation you need before language even becomes useful in those settings.

And honestly, part of it is just that it's an open problem. We don't have the recipe yet the way we do for language. Figuring out what the right data is, what the right objectives are, what "scaling" even means when your tokens are chunks of space rather than words — that's the kind of thing that gets me out of bed.

r003.rationale: It argues for learning spatial structure from visual data, but does not suggest that a world model could develop an accurate account of physics using representations different from human notation.

r004.rationale: The response calls language a highly structured representation and says language models can struggle with spatial reasoning, but does not suggest that language structure constrains the outputs obtainable from models using other modalities.

astra-6.text:
What’s exciting to me is the question of how much intelligence you can get from perception alone. Humans have this rich understanding of the physical world that isn’t necessarily expressed in language. You can look at an unfamiliar object and have some intuition for how it might move, how you could pick it up, or what would happen if you pushed it off a table. It’s hard to describe all of that knowledge in words, but it’s clearly useful knowledge.

So I think there’s a really interesting scientific question here: If you train a model to understand images, video, and spatial relationships, what kinds of representations emerge? Does it learn something about objects, physics, or cause and effect? And can those representations support planning and action?

Language gives you this incredibly powerful window into how people describe the world. But I’m curious about what a model can learn by observing the world directly—especially the things that we see constantly but rarely bother to say.

r004.rationale: It says language offers a powerful window into how people describe the world, but does not suggest that language structure constrains outputs from models using other modalities.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the question of how much intelligence you can get from perception alone. Before you have language, you can still learn that objects persist, that things move in predictable ways, that your actions have consequences. There’s a tremendous amount of structure in the visual world.

And vision forces you to deal with something that language can sometimes let you sidestep: the world is continuous, it’s three-dimensional, and you only ever see part of it. You have to infer what’s behind an object, what might happen next, how a scene would look from another viewpoint. Those feel like really fundamental building blocks of intelligence.

So intellectually, I’m interested in how far that gets you. If a model learns to predict and reason about the visual world, what concepts emerge? And where does it actually need language to go further?
